https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Vandals poured bubble soap and painted graffiti on the second world war memorial in Washington DC on Thursday. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Vandals poured bubble soap and painted graffiti on the second world war memorial in Washington DC on Thursday. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Washington DC Woman arrested after second world war memorial in DC vandalized Suspect faces two felony charges after memorial filled with bubbles and spray-paint reading ‘Clean hands Dirty $’ Edward Helmore Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.43 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A woman was arrested on Friday morning in connection with the vandalization of the National World War Two Memorial on the National Mall in Washington DC , the capital’s federal prosecutor announced. Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, announced mid-morning that a suspect was in custody and had been charged with federal crimes. The memorial had graffiti scrawled on it and the pool polluted with soapy bubbles. “This morning, we are filing two felony charges, Depredation Against Property of the United States and Destruction of Veterans’ Memorials, in Federal District Court against Melissa L Farris, offenses that carry penalties of up to ten years in prison. She is now in custody,” Pirro posted on X , showing two images of a middle-aged woman, one of her with what appears to be a can of spray-paint at the scene. “Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom. Those Americans include my father and grandfather,” Pirro also said in the post. US Park Police had been investigating who graffitied the words “Clean hands dirty $” in red paint on the memorial on Washington DC ’s National Mall for the second world war and vandalized the fountain with soapy bubbles. The US interior department said: “The public should know we will find the person responsible for this disgusting act” and the non-profit Friends of the National World War II Memorial said the site should not be used for political expression. View image in fullscreen Bubble soap on the second world war memorial in Washington DC on Thursday. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/NurPhoto/Shutterstock “There are many places in our country for expression, debate and disagreement,” a statement from the organization said. “A national memorial honoring those who served and those who never returned home should never be used as a canvas for vandalism.” The Veterans of Foreign Wars military service organization said the vandalism was “an act of profound disrespect”. The memorial sits close to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool , which has been the site of controversy in recent months. A contentious upgrade effort ordered by Donald Trump ahead of Fourth of July celebrations for the 250th anniversary of the founding of the US became mired in dispute after new surfacing separated and algae returned . Trump blamed vandals for damage to the pool lining, though prosecutions of individuals alleged to have contributed to the problems have since collapsed, including a high-profile case involving David Hearn , the US Olympian. In early June vandals etched “8647” – a numeric signal of opposition to Trump – on the National Memorial lawn. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said: “Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible.” Leanna Townsend, a visitor to Washington DC from Florida this week, told the Washington Post upon seeing the clouds of bubbles frothing out of the pool at the second world war memorial that they seemed “a little bit juvenile and funny” but described the spray-paint as disrespectful. “I just find it to be in complete distaste, especially for the people that it’s here to honor,” she said. “Shame on the person who thought that’s appropriate. It’s not.” Sonja Weekley, visiting from Alabama, said the bubbles and spray-paint were “ridiculous and very disrespectful” – her grandparents and father-in-law had fought in the second world war, she told the outlet. “This is not political,” she said. “This is for the men and women who fought for us to be free.” In videos posted to Farris’s Facebook account, ​Farris records herself spray-painting the war memorial and asking ‌why she has not been arrested. The criminal complaint filed on Friday quotes ‌Farris as saying: “Someone has to make choices that are different and I am accountable for my actions.” In later videos posted after the incident, she appears disheveled and crying, saying she knows she upset people by her actions but was trying to get help for ‌herself. Trump has clung to claims that the reflecting pool was vandalized , despite charges being dropped . On Friday he posted to his social media platform: “First the Reflecting Pool, now this. We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???” Reuters contributed reporting Explore more on these topics Washington DC US politics US crime Trump administration Second world war US military news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text: ‘We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular,’ Camra’s chief executive said. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular,’ Camra’s chief executive said. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Pubs Problems brewing for the proper pint as Camra membership falls Cost of living has hit campaign group while multinationals are threatening to squeeze out independent breweries Helena Horton Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.01 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F or centuries, the wooden real ale pump has been the hallmark of a good British boozer. But now problems are brewing for the proper pint, as the Campaign for Real Ale has seen its membership sink to an eight-year low and its accounts show it is firmly in the red, making an £800,000 loss last year. Real ale is a traditional draught cask beer, a “living” product that is produced and stored in its cask. It differs from a cold, fizzy lager, in which the yeast is killed and carbon dioxide is added. Real ale contains live yeast so it continues fermenting until it is served. Outside the Devonshire pub in Soho, central London, there is an ever-present horde of drinkers downing pints of Guinness, a stout made by the multinational company Diageo. But the landlord and co-owner Oisín Rogers says: “Real ale is all I drink.” He says: “It is a properly handmade British product produced in exactly the same way it has been for centuries. It has never been industrialised like some of the other drinks that are for sale in bars in London.” His favourite tipple, is, appropriately, a pint of Landlord, made by the family-owned Timothy Taylor brewery in Keighley, West Yorkshire. View image in fullscreen The Devonshire pub in London’s West End. Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty Images Tom Stainer, Camra’s chief executive, says independent breweries are facing unfair competition from multinationals. If you walk into a pub on the high street, you are often confronted with the same few beers, most of which are made by the same large companies, Stainer says. “Our recent beer report highlighted that the beers people want aren’t available in bars because of the ways the huge international brewers operate – they have a stranglehold on the industry,” he says. “We call it an illusion of choice – a lot of people walk into bars and don’t realise everything in front of them is owned by the same big company.” Big brewers ‘misleading drinkers’ over craft beer credentials, says Camra Read more He says these “big global brewers who have deep pockets and huge influence” make it “hard for small brewers to get to market”. The incentives offered to large pub companies include cheap packages for beers, wine and soft drinks, with a multi-year tie-in, and minimum purchase orders where “pubs are forced to sell a certain amount of this product”. Stainer adds: “We have heard of pubs taking off independent beers because they are too popular and stop people buying that product they have a minimum purchase order for.” Camra is calling for the Competition and Markets Authority to investigate the big beer companies’ stranglehold on the market. There are no such problems at the King Charles I pub in King’s Cross. As an independent, community-owned venue, the team can choose what’s on tap. They have a healthy range of cask beers, swapped out every five weeks. Matt Roberts, the manager, says: “I like to choose local beers – today we have one from Southwark, some from Kent and one from the West Midlands. Cask ale is still very popular, it makes up around 30% of our sales. We are lucky we don’t have a big pub company telling us what to sell.” Despite the delicious range of cask ale on offer, including the very drinkable Bankside Blonde by Southwark Brewing Company, Guinness still appears to be the order of the day among the customers. View image in fullscreen Visitors at the Camra Great British Beer festival in 2017. This year’s event was cancelled. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images Camra is facing a nadir: last September it announced it had been forced to cancel its pivotal Great British Beer festival , formerly the largest of its kind in the UK, for the foreseeable future due to financial pressures. Writing in the accounts, the chair, Ash Corbett-Collins, said it had been “one of the most challenging years Camra has faced”, pointing to a restructuring in which “a number of roles were sadly made redundant”. The cost of living crisis is making it more difficult to run a membership organisation, Stainer says. “When you look at your bank balance each month, membership might be something you might economise to offset your huge energy bill or the rise in food prices.” A Camra membership is £35 a year. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: A Jerusalem municipality member stands outside the British consulate on Thursday, the deadline set by Israel for its closure. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters View image in fullscreen A Jerusalem municipality member stands outside the British consulate on Thursday, the deadline set by Israel for its closure. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters Foreign policy British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced UK politics live – latest updates Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Thu 8 Oct 2026 05.20 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 02.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel , with only seven to remain in the building. The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israeli-Palestine conflict. Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign. ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors Read more There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appeared to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics. Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed. The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.” Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of the British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.” He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’”. View image in fullscreen Ed Miliband arriving in Kyiv on Thursday. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Miliband, who is currently visiting Kyiv, said in a statement that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the staffing at the mission in future months. He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks. UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt, regardless of the imminent election outcome. The sources emphasised that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is placed in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to provide vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Vincent Fean, the UK consul general to Palestine between 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.” Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute. The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this. The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory. Israel has also said it would revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them. UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis, as Britain became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments thought was unachievable through his methods. The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel, and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believed this was a matter for international courts to determine. https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-recoverin.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OL4G Pope Leo XIV thanked staff at Gemelli Hospital in Rome for the care they provide for the frail and those suffering disease Image: Vatican Media/AFP Advertisement The Vatican on Friday announced that Pope Leo XIV is swiftly recovering from lung surgery and will make his first public appearance on Sunday, when he will deliver the traditional noontime Angelus Prayer. Vatican representatives did not specify whether he would deliver the prayer at St. Peter's Square or from the hospital. Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said Friday that a recitation from the hospital was a possibility but would depend on Leo's post-operation recovery. Leo, who is 71, shocked the world and its 1.4 billion Catholics last Sunday by announcing that he would be undergoing surgery within days. Two day's later, on October 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after the pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Doctors are awaiting the results of Leo's biopsy, which will tell them about the make-up of the tumor and give insight into whether his cancer has spread, allowing them to determine whether he may need to undergo further treatment, such as radiation or chemotherapy. On Friday, the Vatican said Leo was going about normal activities on his own and released photos of the pontiff saying Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He was seen wearing vestments and standing next to his personal secretary, Edgard Rimaycuna, a Peruvian priest. Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass alongside his personal secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard Rimaycuna Image: Vatican Media/AFP "His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Dr. Luigi Carbone, Leo's personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital. The doctors said blood tests and chest x-rays had confirmed Leo's steady improvement. "At the moment, we have not received any communication from the doctors ⁠regarding ​his discharge, other than what we ​were told from the beginning about a one-week timeframe," a Vatican spokesman ​said. "The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted," said Cardinal Parolin, who added, "We can't make any predictions." One of the first questions raised by Leo's hospitalization and surgery was whether he would be able to go through with a planned papal trip to South America in just a few weeks' time. Though this remains an open question, the Vatican on Friday said planning was "going forward" regardless, releasing the names of those journalists accredited to travel with Leo to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. https://www.digi24.ro/magazin/timp-liber.text: Paul McCartney a intrat în panteonul miliardarilor, revista Forbes estimându-i averea la aproximativ 1,4 miliarde de dolari. Publicaţia i-a acordat lui Sir Paul această distincţie odată cu lansarea buletinului informativ „The Billie”, menţionând că repertoriul său muzical, turneele şi colecţia de artă reprezintă cea mai mare parte a averii sale, potrivit News.ro. Cu o avere netă de 1,4 miliarde de dolari, el este al treilea cel mai bogat muzician din lume, după Taylor Swift, cu 2 miliarde de dolari, şi Jay-Z, cu 2,8 miliarde de dolari. Potrivit revistei Forbes, cea mai mare parte a averii lui McCartney provine de la MPL Communications, compania sa de editare muzicală pe care a înfiinţat-o în 1969 şi care gestionează atât propriul său catalog, cât şi drepturile de autor ale altor artişti. Publicaţia subliniază că achiziţionarea de către McCartney a cataloagelor unor artişti precum Buddy Holly, precum şi a partiturilor muzicalelor de pe Broadway şi a melodiilor tradiţionale de Crăciun, contribuie în mod semnificativ la averea sa, reprezentând aproape un sfert de miliard de dolari. În calitate de membru al formaţiei The Beatles, McCartney primeşte 25% din veniturile holdingului Apple Corps al formaţiei, care generează anual 50 de milioane de dolari din streaming, vânzări de discuri de vinil şi produse promoţionale. Forbes estimează că acest flux de venituri valorează peste 150 de milioane de dolari pentru fiecare membru sau pentru moştenitorii acestora. McCartney câştigă, de asemenea, 10 milioane de dolari pe an din cota sa din drepturile de autor asupra compoziţiilor formaţiei The Beatles, pentru care a luptat în instanţă în ultimele două decenii. Aceasta valorează cel puţin 200 de milioane de dolari. Suma totală a veniturilor sale include turneele mondiale, cel mai recent fiind „Got Back”, care a cuprins 79 de spectacole între 2022 şi 2025, precum şi proprietăţi imobiliare din întreaga lume şi o colecţie de artă care include tablouri de Magritte şi Picasso. McCartney rămâne extrem de activ ca muzician, lansând recent, în luna mai a acestui an, cel de-al 20-lea album solo al său, intitulat „The Boys of Dungeon Lane”. De asemenea, el este protagonistul documentarului „Man on the Run”, regizat de Morgan Neville, care prezintă în detaliu viaţa sa după plecarea din formaţia The Beatles şi înfiinţarea grupului său Wings.
